title: Liquid Penetrant Testing for Pulp & Paper Mills | PT
description: Dye penetrant inspection of stainless and alloy welds in US pulp and paper mills: bleach plants, evaporators, repairs. Crews travel to you. Get a quote.
h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing for Pulp and Paper Mills in the United States
html:
Liquid penetrant testing for pulp and paper mills in the United States is the method for finding surface-breaking cracks and pores on nonmagnetic equipment that magnetic particle cannot examine: stainless bleach plant piping and vessels, evaporator and heat exchanger welds, alloy repairs, pump casings and cladding. Atlantis mobilizes SNT-TC-1A qualified technicians to your mill to examine the welds and surfaces you identify and issues a report with every indication sketched. To scope the work, request a liquid penetrant quote.

Where penetrant earns its place in a pulp mill

A kraft mill is built mostly from carbon steel, but the corrosive stages are not. Bleaching, evaporation, chemical preparation and some recovery duties use austenitic stainless steel, duplex grades and nickel alloys, and none of these respond to a magnet in the way carbon steel does. Liquid penetrant is the standard surface method for those materials because it needs only a clean surface and a flaw that is open to the surface, not a magnetic field.

The same properties limit it. Penetrant cannot find a flaw that is closed or smeared over, it cannot see below the surface, and it says nothing about thinning. For wall loss go to the UT page, and for cracking in carbon steel welds the MT page usually offers a faster examination.

Bleach plant and chemical systems

Bleach plant towers, washers, chemical mix tanks and their piping are often stainless or lined, and chlorides, chlorine dioxide and temperature swings can drive localized corrosion and chloride stress corrosion cracking in austenitic stainless. API 571 describes chloride cracking as fine, branched cracking that starts at the surface, which is exactly what a penetrant examination is suited to show. Welds, heat-affected zones, nozzle connections and any area that has been bent or ground are the first places to look.

Piping spools fabricated or repaired during the outage are a steady source of PT work. A stainless weld repaired in place needs an examination of the root or the first pass in some procedures, and a final surface examination once the weld is finished. The examination points come from the repair procedure, and the mill's engineer sets them. We record each one against the weld identification the mill assigns.

Evaporators, heat exchangers and alloy repairs

Black liquor evaporators and heat exchangers use thin-wall stainless and alloy components whose welds are small and shallow. Tube-to-tubesheet welds, shell nozzle welds and plugs added during an outage all fall into the PT category. A weld that is only a few millimeters across gives little room for error, so the dwell time, the cleaning and the lighting all matter more than on a heavy carbon steel weld.

Pump casings, impellers and valve bodies in alloy materials are examined by penetrant after weld repair or buildup. The report identifies each part by serial number, and surface condition after machining is noted, since a smeared machined surface can hide a crack that only shows after a light etch or removal of smeared metal.

Materials, contaminants and compatibility

Penetrant materials for austenitic stainless steel and nickel-base alloys are controlled for halogen and sulfur content, because residues left on a hot surface can promote cracking. ASME Section V Article 6 requires that the material be certified for contaminant content, and the report records the batch numbers of the penetrant, remover and developer. Carbon steel components in the same mill can use standard materials, but we keep the sets separate so that stainless is never examined with products that were previously used on carbon steel.

Because mill process fluids touch some of these surfaces, post-examination cleaning matters. The remover, developer and penetrant must be flushed or wiped from the part so they cannot reach the process. The cleaning step is written into the procedure and checked at the end of each examination, and the mill decides whether the cleaning is acceptable for its process.

Technique details for mill conditions

  • Penetrant type. Visible dye, solvent removable penetrants are common on site. Fluorescent penetrants give better sensitivity where a dark area and ultraviolet light can be arranged. ASTM E165 and ASME Section V Article 6 define the types and methods.
  • Surface preparation. The surface must be clean, dry and free of scale, oil, paint, weld spatter and smeared metal. Grinding can close a crack, so the procedure may require light etching or a different cleaning step after grinding.
  • Temperature. Without a specially qualified procedure, Article 6 limits the work to a moderate surface temperature range, roughly 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit. Hot, freshly welded equipment is allowed to cool, and cold weather work is done with heating or enclosure when the procedure permits.
  • Dwell time. Penetrant dwell and developer time come from the procedure and the material, and the technician records both for each examination.
  • Lighting. Visible dye needs a minimum light level at the work surface, and fluorescent work needs a dark enclosure and a UV lamp at a stated intensity.
  • Process control. Penetrant system checks, such as comparison blocks where the procedure requires them, are done at the start of work.

Cladding, overlay and weld repairs

Weld overlay and cladding protect carbon steel from corrosive liquors, and the bond line and overlay surface are common penetrant targets. A disbonded or cracked overlay can let liquor reach the base metal, so the examination covers the overlay surface, the fusion line at edges and the transitions around nozzles. Because overlay passes can be rough as deposited, the technician notes whether the surface was ground to a finish suitable for a clear result.

Repairs introduce a second concern: crack-like indications that appear at the start or stop of a bead or at a weld toe. Whether such an indication is accepted depends on the criteria in the code of construction, and the report keeps the indication description separate from any judgment about repair.

Codes, regulators and acceptance

ASME Section V Article 6 is the method, ASTM E165 is the common practice for general industry, and the code of construction supplies acceptance criteria. For pressure vessels that is usually ASME Section VIII, and for boilers ASME Section I with NBIC governing repairs. State boiler law and your inspector of record decide whether the equipment is accepted. Atlantis reports each indication against the criteria you name and does not calculate remaining life, set intervals or judge fitness for service. For background on the method, see our explainer on Article 6 liquid penetrant requirements.

When PT is the wrong choice

Where penetrant fits and where it does not
SituationBetter methodWhy
Cracks in carbon steel weldsMTFaster, sensitive to near-surface flaws
Wall loss on a tank or tubeUTPenetrant gives no thickness
Stainless weld, surface crackingPTMaterial is not magnetic
Porous castings and rough surfacesCase by casePenetrant bleeds out of pores and masks
Cracking below the surfaceNot PTNeeds a volumetric method

Rough, porous or heavily scaled surfaces cause false indications, so the report notes any area where the surface prevented a clear result, and we recommend cleaning or an alternative method for that area.

Reading indications honestly

Penetrant produces three kinds of bleed-out: true linear indications from cracks, rounded indications from porosity, and non-relevant indications from surface geometry such as a sharp weld toe or a machined edge. The technician classifies each one, wipes and re-develops where the procedure allows to confirm a doubtful indication, and records which ones were re-examined. A well-written report separates what was seen from what was decided, because the decision on a relevant indication belongs to the code and the inspector of record.

What the PT report contains

Every report names the component and weld, the procedure and revision, the penetrant system with batch numbers, the dwell and developing times, surface temperature, surface preparation, and the technician and SNT-TC-1A level. Indications are drawn on a sketch with location, size and type, and the report records accept or reject against the named criteria. An ASNT Level III reviews the report before it is issued, and any area not examined, and why, appears in the final summary.

What to send for a quote

  • List of welds or components with tag numbers and drawings or a weld map
  • Material grades, including stainless, duplex or nickel alloys, and thickness
  • Governing code and acceptance criteria, plus any contaminant limits the mill has set
  • Surface condition, coatings, insulation and who prepares the surface
  • Expected surface temperature and working environment, indoors or outdoors
  • Cleaning requirements after examination and any process restrictions
  • Access, permits, site badging and address

Outage coordination in US mills

Penetrant work goes in late in a repair sequence, after grinding and before coating, so it depends on other trades finishing on time. Bleach plant vessels are confined spaces under 29 CFR 1910.146 and the mill's permit program, and chemical residues must be cleared before entry. Atlantis technicians travel to your site with their own penetrant systems and light meters, and the mill provides power, access and permits. For the broader outage framework, see the turnarounds and shutdowns page.

Training your own technicians in PT

For a maintenance team that wants its own surface examination capability, PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training follow SNT-TC-1A, and the penetrant testing simulator offers practice on virtual parts. Your company writes its procedures and certifies its own staff, and our written practice development helps put that in order. Further reading is in the MT versus PT comparison, and the national method page is penetrant testing.

What we do not do here

We do not offer radiography in the US, and we do not offer specialist techniques for cracking in the stainless layer of composite recovery boiler tubes. Penetrant gives no thickness data, so thickness work is a separate scope on the UT page, and weld-specific work is on weld inspection.

faq.q: Can you use penetrant testing on stainless steel in a bleach plant?
faq.a: Yes, that is one of its main uses. Austenitic stainless is not magnetic, so a surface-breaking crack is found with penetrant instead. We use materials controlled for halogen and sulfur content as ASME Section V Article 6 requires.

faq.q: Does liquid penetrant testing find cracks below the surface?
faq.a: No. The flaw must be open to the surface so liquid can enter it. Subsurface flaws and wall loss need ultrasonic or other volumetric examination, and the report notes where surface condition prevented a clear result.

faq.q: What temperature range can you test in?
faq.a: Without a specially qualified procedure the usual range is roughly 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit at the surface. Hot equipment is allowed to cool, and cold weather work needs heat or enclosure if the procedure permits.

faq.q: Do penetrant residues affect our process?
faq.a: They can, so cleaning is part of the procedure. Remover and developer are wiped or flushed away, and the mill decides whether the cleanliness is acceptable before any equipment returns to chemical service.

faq.q: What surface preparation do you need before PT?
faq.a: The surface should be clean, dry and free of scale, oil, paint and spatter. Grinding or blasting can smear metal over cracks, so the procedure may require an etch or another cleaning step before examination.

faq.q: Who accepts or rejects the indications?
faq.a: The code of construction sets the criteria, and your jurisdictional or authorized inspector accepts the equipment. Atlantis records each indication against the criteria you give us and flags relevant ones, and the owner decides on repair.

faq.q: Can you do PT on carbon steel welds too?
faq.a: Yes, though MT is often faster on carbon steel. We use PT on carbon steel where the surface is nonmagnetic after cladding, where access suits penetrant better, or where the procedure calls for it.

faq.q: What do you need from us to quote a PT job?
faq.a: Send the weld or component list with tag numbers, drawings, material grades, governing code, surface condition, temperature, cleaning needs, access method and site badging steps. We will scope time and materials from that.

faq.q: Do you bring your own penetrant materials?
faq.a: Yes. Technicians travel to your site with penetrant, remover and developer, with batch numbers and contaminant certificates available for your records. The mill supplies access, power and lighting and any permits.
